title: Catalog Reconciler
user: Collectors moving a personal catalog between spreadsheets, Homebox, Koillection, or a new system who need to import without silently creating or renumbering records.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Homebox user reports that inventory export omits HB.import_ref, the field needed to preserve identity on re-import.
A separate Homebox import report says import_ref unexpectedly increments asset IDs, demonstrating that catalog migration can mutate collection identity.

recurrence: Two 2025 reports in the same active inventory tool target export/import identity rather than a cosmetic preference; wrong IDs make a collection hard to trust.
current_workaround: Back up a CSV, import into a copy, manually compare counts and identifiers, then repair records or retain the old spreadsheet.
incumbents_and_gap: Homebox and Koillection import data, but neither is a neutral preflight that shows identity collisions, generated IDs, and field loss before writes occur.
smallest_useful_product: Local drag-and-drop CSV/JSON preflight that maps columns, normalizes identifiers, reports added/changed/missing/colliding rows, and emits a reviewed import file. Non-goals: hosting a collection database, scraping marketplaces, or automatic deletion.
success_measure: In a pilot of 20 imports, users catch at least one would-be ID collision or field loss before import in 30% or more of imports.
monetization: one-time — a private local migration utility is best bought when a collector changes systems.
constraints: Process files locally in-browser by default; document CSV formula-injection handling; never require marketplace credentials.
why_distinct: It is a reversible import-diff gate, not another collection catalog.

title: Collection Batch Desk
user: Collectors with hundreds of physical items who need to apply a reviewed tag, location, condition, or collection change to a chosen subset without losing context.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Koillection user explicitly requests multi-selection and editing for tagging, deletion, and assigning a collection.
Homebox tracks an epic for better labeling/tagging across more systems and options, showing the need is not limited to one catalog.

recurrence: Two independent collection platforms have active requests for broader tagging and bulk operations; manual item-by-item curation becomes severe at collection scale.
current_workaround: Export to CSV, use spreadsheet fill-down, or open individual records repeatedly and hope a broad selection was correct.
incumbents_and_gap: Koillection and Homebox own the records but their bulk affordances are incomplete; spreadsheets are powerful but do not show item photos or a change preview.
smallest_useful_product: A local batch-review workspace that accepts a catalog export plus thumbnails, filters a subset, stages tag/location/condition edits, and outputs a patch CSV with undo manifest. Non-goals: collection hosting, image recognition, or direct account automation.
success_measure: At least 70% of pilot sessions stage and export 25+ changes with zero subsequently reverted accidental edits.
monetization: one-time — it is an occasional high-trust curation tool.
constraints: No cloud upload by default; retain original row IDs verbatim; clearly separate destructive operations from export-only changes.
why_distinct: The product is a visual, reversible batch-change layer over existing catalogs rather than a replacement catalog.

title: Meeple Import Doctor
user: Board-game and vinyl collectors importing item URLs into a self-hosted catalog who need a clear answer when an external metadata scraper returns nothing.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A board-game collector says a BoardGameGeek scraper does nothing and exposes no errors or useful logs.
A different collector reports that a Discogs scraper UI appears to work but populates no album data and offers no accessible diagnostics.

recurrence: Two different collection domains and source sites report the same opaque-import failure within nine months; it blocks the setup path for a catalog.
current_workaround: Try another URL, inspect container logs, retype metadata by hand, or abandon the import workflow.
incumbents_and_gap: Koillection offers scraper scripts but not a source-neutral request inspector; BoardGameGeek and Discogs expose data but do not diagnose third-party import mappings.
smallest_useful_product: A browser-based URL inspector with pluggable public-page parsers that displays fetched status, detected fields, selector failures, normalized preview, and a copyable manual-import JSON record. Non-goals: bypassing authentication/anti-bot controls, bulk scraping, or redistributing marketplace data.
success_measure: In 80% of failed test URLs, the user can classify the cause as blocked, missing field, changed markup, or invalid URL in under two minutes.
monetization: free — transparent diagnostics build trust and can seed paid catalog connectors later.
constraints: Respect robots.txt, rate limits, and source terms; no credential collection or anti-bot evasion; parser output must attribute its source.
why_distinct: It diagnoses an import attempt before a catalog writes anything; it is neither a BoardGameGeek clone nor a Discogs client.

title: Edit Sidecar Check
user: Photographers moving edited RAW/DNG files between phone and desktop tools who need to know whether edits, ratings, and tags will survive an export before they lose work.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A photographer describes a Lightroom Android to Snapseed DNG workflow where the second tool shows the original rather than the edited image.
A Lightroom-to-darktable migrator reports that tags disappear when a previously edited DNG is exported to JPEG.

recurrence: Independent mobile and desktop workflows reveal the same portability failure across 2025–26: visual edits and descriptive data are not reliably carried forward.
current_workaround: Export a flattened JPEG/TIFF, keep several originals, or test each app combination manually and discover losses after a batch.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom, Snapseed, and darktable edit images, but none acts as a neutral before/after inspector for rendered pixels, XMP, EXIF, and sidecar semantics across handoffs.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop/web checker that compares source plus sidecar/export, reports pixel-bearing edit data versus portable metadata, and produces a handoff checklist. Non-goals: RAW development, cloud sync, or writing proprietary edits.
success_measure: At least 80% of beta users correctly predict whether ratings, keywords, capture date, and visible edits survive a tested handoff.
monetization: one-time — a specialist preflight tool has clear value at migration and workflow-change moments.
constraints: Local-only file processing; preserve originals; document format-specific limits; do not reverse-engineer or redistribute proprietary editing engines.
why_distinct: It explains interoperability risk; it does not compete as another photo editor.

title: Caption Queue
user: Photographers with large shoots who need a fast, deliberate queue for titles, captions, keywords, and IPTC fields without hand-editing every image in a DAM.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Lightroom Classic user says manual titles, captions, and keywords across large sets are very time-consuming and asks for direct IPTC automation.
A darktable feature request asks for events when tags, geotags, metadata, ratings, and labels change so external workflow automation can react.

recurrence: Two tools expose the same operational need: high-volume metadata work needs structured batching and automation hooks, not per-photo forms.
current_workaround: Copy/paste text, use Lightroom presets, write ad-hoc scripts, or postpone metadata until it never gets completed.
incumbents_and_gap: Lightroom presets and DAM batch tools apply broad changes; automation plugins require setup. The gap is a reviewable task queue with per-image context and standards-valid output.
smallest_useful_product: A local folder/CSV-driven queue that groups images by shoot, offers reusable caption tokens and controlled vocabularies, previews changes, and writes XMP sidecars. Non-goals: generative captions, face recognition, or a full DAM.
success_measure: A pilot photographer completes metadata for a 100-image shoot in less than half their prior recorded time while accepting 95%+ of written sidecars.
monetization: one-time — local offline metadata productivity is a durable pro utility.
constraints: Write sidecars by default rather than modify originals; validate IPTC/XMP escaping; no cloud image upload or LLM-generated claims.
why_distinct: It is a metadata work queue and validator, not a broad image catalog or thin caption generator.

title: Camera Ingest Preflight
user: 360° and mixed-camera photographers who need to see which originals, previews, orientation, camera names, and GPS fields will fail before importing a card into their photo library.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A 360° camera owner asks to use original Insta360 and fisheye RAW files without first stitching them in proprietary desktop software.
A PhotoPrism administrator asks to correct missing or garbled camera make/model without re-indexing.

recurrence: Two 2026 ingest requests show that photographers encounter preventable failures in both media rendering and camera metadata normalization.
current_workaround: Import first, discover failures in a DAM, run vendor software or command-line tools, then re-index or manually correct records.
incumbents_and_gap: PhotoPrism and vendor tools ingest/render media, but neither offers a small card-level readiness report across formats and metadata before a library job begins.
smallest_useful_product: A local folder scanner that reports unsupported formats, embedded-preview availability, 360 projection hints, orientation, duplicate hashes, and camera/GPS anomalies with exportable JSON. Non-goals: stitching 360 media, photo hosting, or replacing a DAM.
success_measure: In a 50-card beta, the tool identifies 95% of files that a configured downstream library would reject or misclassify before import.
monetization: freemium — a free local scan builds trust; paid report presets for DAM migrations can fund maintenance.
constraints: Read-only by default; use documented media parsers; do not ship proprietary codecs; preserve location privacy in reports.
why_distinct: It makes an ingest decision observable before a DAM commit instead of becoming another photo library.

title: Route Intent Planner
user: Cyclists and ride leaders who know the roads or paths they intend to use and need a route planner that preserves those choices instead of silently redrawing them.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A user planning a known club route says Organic Maps eagerly completes their waypoint route into something that makes no sense.
A cyclist reports brief but unnecessary detours produced by bike routing profiles, with reproducible examples.

recurrence: Two routing engines receive concrete 2026 reports where automated optimization overrides local route intent; this matters especially for group rides.
current_workaround: Add excessive waypoints, draw a line in a separate map, export GPX, and repeatedly inspect segments for detours.
incumbents_and_gap: Organic Maps and BRouter calculate routes well but optimize per profile. Neither is centered on declaring must-use corridors and explaining every deviation from them.
smallest_useful_product: A GPX/web planner that accepts a rough trace or named mandatory segments, locks those corridors, optimizes only gaps, and flags off-intent sections. Non-goals: turn-by-turn navigation, social feed, or proprietary map tiles.
success_measure: At least 85% of routes made by ride leaders need no post-export correction to preserve their selected roads/paths.
monetization: one-time — route planning is occasional and should export standard GPX without a subscription trap.
constraints: Use OpenStreetMap-compatible data/licensing; clearly label routing as advisory; cache map data and respect tile-provider policy.
why_distinct: The core object is user-declared route intent and deviations, not a new general-purpose map.

title: Cycle Legal Check
user: Cyclists riding speed pedelecs or crossing local restrictions who need a pre-ride explanation of where their GPX/profile conflicts with route access rules.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A BRouter user reports a downhill bicycle route that is legally closed to bikes despite correct OSM settings and notes a potential fine.
A Belgian rider requests a speed-pedelec-aware profile because 45 km/h e-bikes have separate traffic rules and are tricky to navigate.

recurrence: Two independent BRouter reports spanning 2025–26 show access legality is profile- and jurisdiction-sensitive, with real safety and fine consequences.
current_workaround: Trust a generic bicycle profile, research restrictions separately, or discover an illegal segment while riding.
incumbents_and_gap: BRouter profiles and navigation apps use OSM tags, but riders lack a compact legal-risk report that calls out uncertain, prohibited, or vehicle-specific sections before departure.
smallest_useful_product: A GPX analyzer that compares route edges against selected vehicle class and region rules, highlights access conflicts/unknowns, links to underlying OSM tags, and exports a review checklist. Non-goals: legal advice, live navigation, or automated map editing.
success_measure: In a labeled test set of 100 routes, it flags 90%+ of known prohibited/vehicle-mismatched segments with an explicit uncertainty state.
monetization: freemium — basic GPX checks can be free while maintained regional rule packs warrant paid access.
constraints: Must state that it is not legal advice; record rule-source dates; comply with OSM attribution and data licenses; do not claim complete coverage.
why_distinct: It audits a planned route’s access assumptions rather than competing as another navigation app.

title: Cue Audit
user: Cyclists exporting GPX for unfamiliar or out-and-back rides who need to find missing turns and ambiguous overlapping track direction before sharing a route.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A BRouter/Cruiser report describes missing turn instructions where a road continues but a turn is still required.
A round-trip rider asks how to distinguish outbound from return lines when an overlapping track has no direction markers.

recurrence: Independent routing users report instruction and direction ambiguity in 2025–26; these are high-severity failures once a route is shared or ridden offline.
current_workaround: Inspect GPX manually, add waypoints by hand, carry a separate cue sheet, or zoom/pan while riding.
incumbents_and_gap: BRouter calculates routes and Organic Maps displays tracks, but neither is a portable QA pass that scores cue coverage and overlap ambiguity in an exported GPX.
smallest_useful_product: Offline GPX linter that detects sharp same-road turns, close overlapping/reversed segments, long no-cue stretches, and missing directionality; emits a printable cue-review sheet. Non-goals: live navigation, route generation, or map editing.
success_measure: On 50 known problematic GPX files, the linter identifies 85%+ of manually labeled cue/overlap hazards with under 20% false positives.
monetization: one-time — riders can use it locally before events or trips without continuing service cost.
constraints: GPX stays local; findings are advisory; support standard GPX extensions without assuming any vendor’s private schema.
why_distinct: It validates shareable route instructions rather than offering another basemap or cycling computer.

title: Bar Notes
user: Self-directed instrumentalists working from scores who need to capture a concrete next action at a bar and turn those notes into a realistic practice session.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A musician practicing alone after years of lessons describes hitting a wall without guidance and struggling to sustain non-piece practice.
A MuseScore user asks for score memory notes such as “fix bar 37,” explaining that they currently use paper notes.

recurrence: A 2026 learner asks for structure after losing teacher feedback, while a separate notation user asks for bar-specific memory notes; both identify the gap between a score and a practice plan.
current_workaround: Write comments on paper, keep a generic practice journal, or repeatedly rediscover trouble bars during the next session.
incumbents_and_gap: MuseScore focuses on notation and generic habit trackers track minutes. Neither makes score location, next action, and spaced review a lightweight shared object.
smallest_useful_product: Local PWA that imports a score PDF/image, anchors short notes to bar/page regions, schedules unresolved notes, and runs a distraction-free session queue. Non-goals: score engraving, audio transcription, social coaching, or diagnosis of technique.
success_measure: At least 60% of pilot musicians reopen and resolve 10+ bar notes over four weeks, with a reported reduction in forgotten trouble spots.
monetization: one-time — musicians should retain private score annotations without a recurring account fee.
constraints: User supplies only scores they may store; local-first encrypted export; no copyrighted score catalog or sharing marketplace.
why_distinct: It connects actionable score annotations to practice recall, not a generic notes app or notation editor.

title: Tempo Lab
user: Musicians practicing timing and expressive playback who need controlled tempo variation and repeatable drills rather than a fixed click or destructive notation hacks.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A musician explicitly asks about the value of practising with a randomly fluctuating metronome.
A MuseScore request says individual playback timing currently requires tiny tuplets, extra tempo changes, or editing exported audio afterwards.

recurrence: Separate 2026 requests seek controlled timing variation in practice and note-level playback, while current workarounds distort the score or leave the notation tool.
current_workaround: Use a fixed metronome, manually change tempo, create notation hacks, or edit audio after export.
incumbents_and_gap: Standard metronomes hold a tempo and notation apps preserve notation. The gap is a practice-first session builder that varies tempo predictably and records what variation was attempted.
smallest_useful_product: Offline web metronome with bounded random drift, ramp, delayed-beat, and recovery drills; save/share a tiny session preset and export a practice log. Non-goals: AI listening assessment, music streaming, or notation editing.
success_measure: At least 50% of weekly active beta users save and replay three or more named drills within 30 days.
monetization: free — a privacy-respecting practice primitive benefits from broad adoption; optional one-time preset packs can follow.
constraints: Keep audio timing deterministic and functional offline; avoid medical/performance claims; provide accessible visual/haptic alternatives.
why_distinct: It is a reproducible timing-drill instrument, not a thin AI music tutor or a standard click-track clone.

title: Bird Name Bridge
user: Multilingual birders planning a trip or sharing sightings who need to map one species across local/common/scientific names without losing the original observation wording.

evidence.quote_or_summary: Taxon Bridge’s 2026 product issue identifies cross-language birding, Share Sheet, and Merlin workflows as its core user value.
An Organic Maps fork user asks for birding sites, such as observation towers, to be more visible.

recurrence: Two 2026 birding-adjacent requests surface the same fragmentation: names, sighting tools, and where-to-bird context do not travel cleanly together.
current_workaround: Search common and Latin names separately, copy/paste between Merlin/eBird/maps, and maintain personal translation notes.
incumbents_and_gap: Merlin/eBird handle identification and checklists; maps show places. They do not provide a minimal offline bridge that preserves multilingual names alongside personal place notes.
smallest_useful_product: Offline PWA with a downloadable regional taxonomy/name pack, one-species lookup across languages, personal aliases, and share cards linked to an optional saved observation-place note. Non-goals: automated species identification, eBird submission, or crowdsourced rarity alerts.
success_measure: In a multilingual beta, 70% of users find a target species from a non-primary-language name in under 15 seconds and save at least five aliases/notes.
monetization: free — regional name data should be broadly accessible; optional curated offline packs can support maintenance if licensing permits.
constraints: Use only taxonomy/name datasets with compatible licenses and attribution; no claim of identification certainty; location notes remain local by default.
why_distinct: It is a multilingual lookup and context bridge, not another AI bird identifier or citizen-science platform.
